papers.title: Where the SRAM Goes: Per-Symbol Attribution of Static Memory in FreeRTOS-C and Embassy-Rust IoT Firmware on a 64 KB RISC-V Microcontroller
authors: Romi Fadli, Jan Everhard Riwurohi, Wahyu Ramadani Putri Utami, Zulfa Malika Amana
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2610.21064v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Selecting a firmware stack for a memory-constrained microcontroller is usually guided by aggregate binary sizes, which report how much SRAM a build consumes but not where it goes or why. We address that gap with a per-symbol attribution method that decomposes static RAM into architectural categories - scheduler heap, network buffers and pools, task stacks, and linker-reserved regions - by bounding sized ELF symbols to the .data, .bss and .stack section ranges. The method is validated by reconciling every category sum exactly against the size-based totals for all sixteen builds. papers.title: Arcal\'{i}s: Accelerating Remote Procedure Calls Using a L\'{i}ghtweight Near-Cache Solution
authors: Johnson Umeike (University of Maryland, College Park), Pongstorn Maidee (AMD Research,Advanced Development), Bahar Asgari (University of Maryland, College Park)
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2602.12596v5 Announce Type: replace 
Abstract: Modern microservices increasingly depend on high-performance remote procedure calls (RPCs) to coordinate fine-grained, distributed computation. As network bandwidths continue to scale, the CPU overhead associated with RPC processing, particularly serialization, deserialization, and protocol handling, has become a critical bottleneck. This challenge is exacerbated by fast user-space networking stacks such as DPDK, which expose RPC processing as the dominant performance limiter. While prior hardware accelerators have explored NIC-attached and FPGA-based offload, these approaches remain farther from the cache hierarchy, so the frequent data accesses during RPC processing each pay an extra interconnect traversal cost that inflates RPC time.

papers.title: Foundations of Hardware-Software Leakage Contracts
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2610.20754v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Microarchitectural attacks such as Spectre and Meltdown undermine security by exploiting software-visible side effects of microarchitectural optimizations like caches and speculative execution. To use modern hardware securely, programmers must take into account the security implications of these optimizations. Yet instruction set architectures (ISAs)---the conventional abstraction layer between hardware and software---are ill-suited for secure programming: by design, they abstract from microarchitectural details and therefore fail to reflect their security consequences.

Abstract: Meta deploys a heterogeneous fleet comprising NVIDIA GPUs, AMD GPUs, and proprietary MTIA accelerators to reduce costs and mitigate vendor lock-in. However, the extensive history of NVIDIA-specific optimizations hinders performance portability to other hardware. This paper presents our methods for optimizing alternative accelerators, using AMD Instinct MI350X versus NVIDIA B200 for recommendation model training as a case study. We propose three reusable principles. First, hardware-model co-design is essential: rather than directly porting models from NVIDIA GPUs, revising model structures and software recipes allows full exploitation of accelerator-specific strengths (e.g., MI350X's 1.6x HBM capacity relative to B200). papers.title: A Black-Box Positioning Solution for Effortless Integration in Wearable Navigation
authors: Anh-Van Vu, Changmin Sung, Dongsoo Han
papers.abstract:
arXiv:2610.21353v1 Announce Type: cross 
Abstract: Accurate localization is critical for a wide range of applications, including navigation, augmented reality, safety management, and healthcare. However, achieving accurate positioning remains challenging, especially in GPS-degraded environments. Pedestrian Dead Reckoning (PDR), which estimates position based on inertial sensor data, offers a promising alternative but typically demands substantial effort in algorithm design and system integration. This complexity often leads to prolonged development timelines and elevated costs.
